scenes.tts: A rat ignores a light touch on its paw. Days after a nerve injury, the same touch makes it pull away. Why?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Touch That Hurts. A rat silhouette with one hind paw highlighted. Question on screen: why does a touch it ignored now make it pull away?
scenes.narration: A rat ignores a light touch on its paw. Days after a nerve injury, the same touch makes it pull away. Why?

scenes.tts: The rat stands on a wire-mesh floor. A thin filament presses up against its hind paw. The paw stays down.
scenes.visual: Side view: a rat on a wire-mesh floor; a thin filament rises from below and bends against the hind paw. The paw stays flat. Label: before surgery.
scenes.narration: The rat stands on a wire-mesh floor. A thin filament presses up against its hind paw. The paw stays down.

scenes.tts: Then comes a spared nerve injury. Two branches of the nerve to the paw are cut, and one is spared.
scenes.visual: Schematic of a leg nerve splitting into three branches toward the paw. Two branches get cut marks; the third stays intact and is labelled spared. Title: spared nerve injury.
scenes.narration: Then comes a spared nerve injury. Two branches of the nerve to the paw are cut, and one is spared.

scenes.tts: Days later, the same filament makes the paw lift.
scenes.visual: Back to the mesh floor. The same filament touches the paw, and the paw lifts sharply. Label: days after injury, same filament.
scenes.narration: Days later, the same filament makes the paw lift.

scenes.tts: Allodynia means pain from a stimulus that normally does not hurt. A rat cannot tell us, so the paw lift stands in for it.
scenes.visual: Definition card: allodynia = pain from a stimulus that normally does not hurt. Smaller line below: in rodents, the stand-in is a paw that withdraws from a light touch.
scenes.narration: Allodynia means pain from a stimulus that normally does not hurt. A rat cannot tell us, so the paw lift stands in for it.

scenes.tts: The touches come from filaments of rising stiffness, pressed over repeated trials. Many labs take the force that lifts the paw half the time. That is the withdrawal threshold.
scenes.visual: A row of von Frey filaments from thin to thick. Each is pressed several times; ticks mark lifts and crosses mark no lift. A marker settles where about half the presses give a lift. Label: withdrawal threshold, estimated over repeated trials.
scenes.narration: The touches come from filaments of rising stiffness, pressed over repeated trials. Many labs take the force that lifts the paw half the time. That is the withdrawal threshold.

scenes.tts: Plot that threshold over time. In sham-operated rats it stays flat. In injured rats it falls within days, and stays low.
scenes.visual: Illustrative plot, labelled made-up shape, not data: withdrawal threshold against time. A grey sham line stays flat. A coloured injured line drops after surgery and stays low for weeks.
scenes.narration: Plot that threshold over time. In sham-operated rats it stays flat. In injured rats it falls within days, and stays low.

scenes.tts: When a treatment is said to reverse allodynia, it pushes that curve back up, often only for a while.
scenes.visual: Same plot. An arrow marks a treatment; the injured line rises toward baseline, then sags again. Label: reversed the allodynia.
scenes.narration: When a treatment is said to reverse allodynia, it pushes that curve back up, often only for a while.

scenes.tts: Two other words matter. Hyperalgesia is more pain to a stimulus that already hurts. Spontaneous pain comes with no applied stimulus.
scenes.visual: Two definition cards beside allodynia: hyperalgesia = more pain to a stimulus that already hurts; spontaneous pain = pain with no applied stimulus, hard to measure in animals.
scenes.narration: Two other words matter. Hyperalgesia is more pain to a stimulus that already hurts. Spontaneous pain comes with no applied stimulus.

scenes.tts: Notice what is measured. Most rodent papers on allodynia report a withdrawal threshold, which is a reflex. Hold on to that.
scenes.visual: The lifting paw, with a tag: what is usually measured = a withdrawal threshold, a reflex. A small pin icon: hold on to this.
scenes.narration: Notice what is measured. Most rodent papers on allodynia report a withdrawal threshold, which is a reflex. Hold on to that.

scenes.tts: So is persistent pain an alarm that never switched off, or a changed nervous system? Which would you pick?
scenes.visual: Two doors: alarm stuck on, or the nervous system changed. A question mark between them.
scenes.narration: So is persistent pain an alarm that never switched off, or a changed nervous system? Which would you pick?

scenes.tts: The answer is both. After injury, some sensory neurons fire with no stimulus. So the alarm wiring itself has changed.
scenes.visual: Both doors open onto one picture: a sensory neuron firing spikes with no stimulus drawn. Labels: after injury; the alarm wiring has changed.
scenes.narration: The answer is both. After injury, some sensory neurons fire with no stimulus. So the alarm wiring itself has changed.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea to carry through. After a nerve injury, pain persists because the rules of the system have changed.
scenes.visual: A three-level schematic, all grey: dorsal root ganglion, dorsal horn of the spinal cord, brain. Title: the one idea, the rules have changed.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea to carry through. After a nerve injury, pain persists because the rules of the system have changed.

scenes.tts: First, sensory neurons make signals with no stimulus.
scenes.visual: The ganglion level lights up; spikes run along an axon with no stimulus at the skin.
scenes.narration: First, sensory neurons make signals with no stimulus.

scenes.tts: Second, in rats, the dorsal horn loses inhibition. In a simple model, a light touch that used to fall short can then fire a pain-signalling neuron.
scenes.visual: The dorsal horn level lights up. An inhibitory synapse fades; a feather-icon touch input now reaches a threshold line on a pain-signalling neuron, which fires. Corner label: illustrative model, not a recording.
scenes.narration: Second, in rats, the dorsal horn loses inhibition. In a simple model, a light touch that used to fall short can then fire a pain-signalling neuron.

scenes.tts: Third, in rodents, immune cells help hold that change, by routes that differ with sex and compartment.
scenes.visual: Small immune cells appear around the dorsal horn and the ganglion, with labels: help hold the change; routes differ with sex and compartment.
scenes.narration: Third, in rodents, immune cells help hold that change, by routes that differ with sex and compartment.

scenes.tts: Fourth, separate brain circuits set how unpleasant the result is, apart from the reflex.
scenes.visual: The brain level lights up. The paw-withdrawal loop is drawn at the spinal cord: touch in, cord, paw lifts. A separate arrow ascends from the cord to the brain and ends at an unpleasantness dial. A thin descending arrow from brain to cord shows that the brain can modulate the cord.
scenes.narration: Fourth, separate brain circuits set how unpleasant the result is, apart from the reflex.

scenes.tts: Most of this comes from rodent nerve-injury models. In people, the evidence is association.
scenes.visual: Scope card: rodents, nerve-injury models; people, associations. Small note: not established here for nociplastic pain or arthritis, where ongoing input and changed processing can coexist.
scenes.narration: Most of this comes from rodent nerve-injury models. In people, the evidence is association.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the alarm wiring changed, and so did the rules for what counts as a pain signal.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the full three-level schematic lit, with the line: the wiring changed, and so did the rules.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the alarm wiring changed, and so did the rules for what counts as a pain signal.
